元和二年，遷兵部郎中。 與許孟容、韋貫之等受詔刪定制敕，成三十卷，奏行用。 改秘書少監，復兼史館修撰。 尋奉詔與獨孤郁、韋處厚同修《德宗實錄》。 五年，書成奏禦，以功拜右諫議大夫。 明年監修國史裴垍罷相，李吉甫再入，以乂垍之修撰，改授太常少卿。 久之，遷秘書監。
In the second year of Yuanhe he was transferred to Director in the Ministry of War. Together with Xu Mengrong, Wei Guanzhi, and others he received an edict to revise and fix regulations and edicts; thirty juan were completed, submitted, and put into use. He was reassigned as Vice Director of the Palace Library and again served concurrently as historiographer in the History Institute. Soon he received an edict together with Dugu Yu and Wei Chuhou to revise the Veritable Records of Dezong. In the fifth year the book was completed and submitted to the throne; for this service he was appointed Right Remonstrance Official. The next year Pei Ji, supervising editor of the national history, was removed as chancellor; Li Jifu entered again; because Yi was Ji's compiler, he was reassigned as Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. After a long time he was transferred to Director of the Palace Library.
71
乂性樸直，不能事人，或遇權臣專政，輒數歲不遷官。 在朝垂三十年，前後每有大政事、大議論，宰執不能裁決者，必召以咨訪。 乂征引典故，以參時事，多合其宜，然亦以此自滯。 而好學不倦，老而彌篤，雖甚寒暑，手不釋卷。 旁通百家，尤精歷代沿革。 家藏書一萬五千卷。 本名武，因憲宗召對，奏曰，「陛下已誅群寇，偃武修文，臣名於義未允，請改名乂。」 上忻然從之。 時帝方用兵兩河，乂亦因此諷諭耳。 乂居史任二十年，所著《大唐宰輔錄》七十卷、《淩煙閣功臣》、《秦府十八學士》、《史臣》等傳四十卷。 長慶元年卒，年七十五，贈禮部尚書，謚曰懿。 子係、伸、偕、仙、佶。
Yi's nature was plain and upright; he could not serve men; when he encountered powerful ministers monopolizing government, he would go several years without transfer. In court for nearly thirty years, whenever there were great state affairs or great debates that the chancellors could not decide, he was always summoned for consultation. Yi cited canonical precedents to compare with current affairs; mostly they fit what was fitting, yet he also on this account stagnated himself. Yet he loved learning without tiring; in old age he became only more earnest; even in extreme cold and heat his hand did not release his scroll. He broadly mastered the hundred schools and was especially expert in the changes of successive dynasties. His household collection held fifteen thousand juan of books. His original name was Wu; because Xianzong summoned him for audience, in memorial he stated: "Your Majesty has already executed the bandit rebels and is now laying down arms to cultivate culture — my name no longer suits the meaning; I request to change it to Yi." The emperor gladly assented. At the time the emperor was just then using troops on the two He regions; Yi also on this account offered indirect counsel. Yi held historiographical office for twenty years; works he authored include the "Record of Tang Chancellors" in seventy juan, biographies of the Lingyan Pavilion meritorious ministers, the eighteen scholars of the Prince of Qin's household, and historiographers — forty juan in all. He died in the first year of Changqing at the age of seventy-five; he was posthumously awarded Minister of Rites and given the posthumous title Yi. His sons were Xi, Shen, Xie, Xian, and Ji.
72
係，太和初授昭應尉，直史館。 二年，拜右拾遺、史館修撰，典實有父風。 與同職沈傳師、鄭浣、陳夷行、李漢等受詔撰《憲宗實錄》。 四年，書成奏禦，轉尚書工部員外，遷本司郎中，仍兼史職。 宰相宋申錫為北軍羅織，罪在不測，係與諫官崔玄亮泣諫於玉階之下，申錫亦減死，時論稱之。 開成中，轉諫議大夫。 武宗朝，李德裕用事，惡李漢，以係與漢僚婿，出為桂管都護禦觀察使。 中宗即位，征拜給事中、集賢殿學士、判院事。 轉吏部侍郎，改左丞。 出為興元節度使，入為刑部尚書。 俄檢校戶部尚書、鳳翔尹，充鳳翔隴節度使，入為兵部尚書。 以弟伸為丞相，懇辭朝秩，檢校尚書左僕射、襄州刺史、山南東道節度使，封淮陽縣開國公，食邑五百戶。
Xi, in the early Taihe era, was appointed bailiff of Zhaoying and served directly in the History Institute. In the second year he was appointed Right Remonstrance Official and historiographer in the History Institute; in handling substance he had his father's manner. Together with colleagues Shen Chuanshi, Zheng Huan, Chen Yixing, and Li Han he received an edict to compile the Veritable Records of Xianzong. In the fourth year the book was completed and submitted to the throne; he was transferred to Vice Director in the Ministry of Public Works in the Ministry of Works, then to Director in his home ministry, still concurrently holding historiographical office. When Chancellor Song Shenxi was framed by the Northern Armies and his guilt was uncertain, Xi together with remonstrance officials Cui Xuanliang wept and remonstrated below the jade steps; Shenxi also had his death sentence reduced, and public opinion praised this. In the Kaicheng era he was transferred to Remonstrance Official. In the Wuzong era Li Deyu held power and hated Li Han; because Xi was son-in-law to Han's colleague, he was sent out as Military Commissioner, Surveillance Commissioner, and Defense Commissioner of Guiguan. When Zhongzong took the throne, he was summoned and appointed Supervising Secretary, academician of the Hall of Assembled Worthies, and acting director of the institute. He was transferred to Vice Minister of Personnel and reassigned as Left Vice Director. He went out as military commissioner of Xingyuan and entered as Minister of Justice. Soon he was made Acting Minister of Revenue, Intendant of Fengxiang, and Military Commissioner of Fengxiang and Long, and entered as Minister of War. Because his younger brother Shen became chancellor, he earnestly declined court rank and was made Acting Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Prefect of Xiang Prefecture, and Military Commissioner of Shannan East Circuit, enfeoffed as Duke of Huaiyang County with a fief of five hundred households.
73
伸，登進士第，歷佐使府。 大中初入朝，右補闕、史館修撰，轉中書舍人，召入翰林為學士。 自員外郎中，至戶部侍郎、學士承旨，轉兵部侍郎。 大中末，中書侍郎、平章事。
Shen passed the jinshi examination and successively served as staff officer in commissioner offices. In the early Dazhong era he entered court as Right Supplementation Official and historiographer in the History Institute, was transferred to Secretariat Drafter, and was summoned into the Hanlin Academy as academician. From vice director and director he rose to Vice Minister of Revenue and chief academician, then was transferred to Vice Minister of War. At the end of Dazhong he was Vice Director of the Secretariat and Associate Councilor of State.
74
仙、佶，皆至刺史。
Xian and Ji both rose to prefect.
75
偕，有史才，以父任歷官左拾遺、史館修撰，轉補闕。 咸通中，與同職盧耽、牛叢等受詔修《文宗實錄》。
Xie had talent for history; through his father's office he successively served as Left Remonstrance Official and historiographer in the History Institute, and was transferred to Supplementation Official. In the Xiantong era he together with colleagues Lu Dan and Niu Cong received an edict to revise the Veritable Records of Wenzong.
76
蔣氏世以儒史稱，不以文藻為事，唯伸及系子兆有文才，登進士第，然不為文士所譽。 與柳氏、沈氏父子相繼修國史實錄，時推良史，京師云《蔣氏日曆》，士族靡不家藏焉。
The Jiang clan for generations was famed for Confucian learning and historiography and did not make literary ornament their business; only Shen and Xi's son Zhao had literary talent and passed the jinshi examination, yet they were not praised by literary men. Along with the Liu and Shen families, father and son in succession edited the national history and veritable records; contemporaries hailed them as exemplary historians. In the capital the work was known as the Chiang Family Calendar, and every gentry household kept a copy.
77
柳登
Liu Deng
78
柳登，字成伯，河東人。 父芳，肅宗朝史官，與同職韋述受詔添修吳兢所撰《國史》； 殺青未竟而述亡，芳緒述凡例，勒成《國史》一百三十卷。 上自高祖，下止乾元，而敘天寶後事，絕無倫類，取舍非工，不為史氏所稱。 然芳勤於記註，含毫罔倦。 屬安、史亂離，國史散落，編綴所聞，率多闕漏。 上元中坐事徙黔中，遇內官高力士亦貶巫州，遇諸途。 芳以所疑禁中事，咨於力士。 力士說開元、天寶中時政事，芳隨口誌之。 又以《國史》已成，經於奏禦，不可復改，乃別撰《唐歷》四十卷，以力士所傳，載於年歷之下。 芳自永寧尉、直史館，轉拾遺、補闕、員外郎，皆居史任，位終右司郎中、集賢學士。
Liu Deng, styled Chengbi, was from Hedong. His father Fang served as a historiographer under Emperor Suzong and, with his colleague Wei Shu, was ordered to supplement and revise Wu Jing's National History; before the final editing was complete Wei Shu died; Fang followed Shu's outline and completed the National History in one hundred thirty scrolls. It covered the reign from Gaozu down to the Qianyuan era, but its account of events after the Tianbao period lacked all order and proportion, and its editorial choices were poor; historians did not commend it. Yet Fang was tireless in recording and annotating, never wearying at his desk. During the An and Shi rebellions the national history was scattered and lost, and what he pieced together from hearsay was largely incomplete. In the Shangyuan era he was punished and exiled to Qianzhong; on the road he met the inner-palace eunuch Gao Lishi, likewise demoted to Wuzhou. Fang asked Lishi about matters of the inner palace that puzzled him. Lishi recounted political affairs of the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras, and Fang recorded them as he spoke. Since the National History was already complete and had been presented to the throne, it could not be revised; he therefore separately compiled the Tang Annals in forty scrolls, recording Lishi's account under the yearly entries. Fang rose from aide of Yongning and direct appointment to the Historiography Institute through remonstrance and reviser and external official—all historiographical posts—and ended as Right Director in the Ministry of Revenue and Academician of the Hall of Assembled Worthies.
79
登少嗜學，與弟冕鹹以該博著稱。 登年六十餘，方從宦遊，累遷至膳部郎中。 元和初，為大理少卿，與刑部侍郎許孟容等七人，奉詔刪定開元已後敕格。 再遷右庶子，以衰病改秘書監，不拜，授右散騎常侍致仕。 長慶二年卒，時九十餘，輟朝一日，贈工部尚書。 弟冕。
Deng loved learning from youth; he and his younger brother Mian were both renowned for encyclopedic learning. Deng was over sixty before he took up office on the circuit; he rose through repeated promotions to Director in the Ministry of Rites. At the opening of Yuanhe he served as Vice Director of the Court of Judicial Review and, with Vice Minister of Justice Xu Mengrong and six others, was ordered to abridge and codify statutes and regulations issued after Kaiyuan. Promoted again to Right Vice Director of the Crown Prince's Household, he declined transfer to Director of the Palace Library on account of age and illness and was granted retirement as Right Regular Palace Attendant. He died in the second year of Changqing, aged over ninety; the court suspended audiences for one day and posthumously honored him as Minister of Works. His younger brother was Mian.
80
冕，文史兼該，長於吏職。 貞元初，為太常博士。 二年，昭德王皇后之喪，論皇太子服紀。 左補闕穆質請依禮周期而除，冕與同職張薦等奏議曰：
Mian was accomplished in both letters and history and excelled in administrative affairs. At the opening of Zhenyuan he served as Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. In the second year, at the mourning for Empress Zhaode, the question arose of what mourning the crown prince should wear. Left Reviser Mu Zhi asked that mourning be removed after the ritual period; Mian, together with Zhang Jian and others of the same office, submitted a memorial stating:
81
準《開元禮》，子為母齊衰三年，此王公已下服紀。 皇太子為皇后喪服，國禮無聞。 昔晉武帝元皇后崩，其時亦疑太子所服。 杜元凱奏議曰：「古者天子三年之喪，既葬除服。 魏氏革命，亦以既葬為節。 故天子諸侯之禮，嘗已具矣，惡其害己而削去其節。 今其存者唯《士喪禮》一篇，戴勝之記錯雜其內，亦難以取正。 皇太子配二尊，與國為體，固宜卒哭而除服。」 於是山濤、魏舒並同其議，晉朝從之。 歷代遵行，垂之不朽。
According to the Kaiyuan Rites, a son wears unhemmed sackcloth mourning for his mother for three years—this is the mourning prescribed for kings and dukes downward. The state rites say nothing about mourning dress for the crown prince at an empress's funeral. In former times, when Empress Yuan of Emperor Wu of Jin died, there was likewise doubt about the crown prince's mourning dress. Du Yuankai submitted a memorial stating, "In antiquity the Son of Heaven observed three years of mourning and removed mourning garments after the burial. When Wei transformed the mandate, it likewise took burial as the limit. Thus the rites for Son of Heaven and feudal lords had once been fully established, but rulers hated the burden on themselves and cut away the limits. What survives now is only the one scroll of Rites of the Scholar's Mourning, with Dai Sheng's records jumbled within it, and it is hard to take as authoritative. The crown prince is paired with two exalted persons and is one body with the state; he should indeed end wailing and remove mourning dress." Thereupon Shan Tao and Wei Shu both agreed, and the Jin court followed their view. Successive dynasties observed it, and it has endured ever since.
82
臣謹按實錄，文德皇后以貞觀十年九月崩，十一月葬，至十一年正月，除晉王，治為并州都督。 晉王即高宗在籓所封，文德皇后幼子，據其命官，當已除之義也。 今請皇太子依魏、晉故事，為大行皇后喪服，葬而虞，虞而卒哭，卒哭而除，心喪終制，庶存厭降之禮。
Your subjects respectfully examine the veritable record: Empress Wende died in the ninth month of the tenth year of Zhenguan and was buried in the eleventh month; by the first month of the eleventh year the Prince of Jin was released from mourning and appointed concurrently as Governor-General of Bing. The Prince of Jin was the title Gaozong held in the fief; he was Empress Wende's youngest son, and from his appointment to office it is clear he had already been released from mourning. We now request that the crown prince follow Wei and Jin precedent in mourning for the late empress: burial, then the offering rite; the offering rite, then the end of wailing; the end of wailing, then removal of dress—with inner mourning carried through the full period, thus preserving the rite of suppressed mourning.
83
事下中書，宰臣召問禮官曰：「《語》云：『子食於有喪者之側，未嘗飽也。』 今豈可令皇太子衰服侍膳，至於既葬乎？ 準令，群臣齊衰，給假三十日即公除。 約於此制，更審議之。」 張薦曰：「請依宋、齊間皇后為父母服三十日公除例，為皇太子喪服之節。」 三十日公除詣於正內，則服墨慘，歸至本院，衰麻如故。 穆質曰：「杜元凱既葬除服之論，不足為法。 臣愚以為遵三年之制則太重，從三十日之變太輕，唯行古之道，以周年為定。」 詔宰臣與禮官定可否。 宰臣以穆質所奏問博士，冕對曰：「準《禮》，三年喪，無貴賤一也。 豈有以父母貴賤而差降喪服之節乎？ 且《禮》有公門脫齊衰，《開元禮》皇后為父母服十三月，其稟朝旨，十三日而除； 皇太子為外祖父母服五月，其從朝旨，則五日而除。 所以然者，恐喪服侍奉，有傷至尊之意也。 故從權制，昭著國章，公門脫衰，義亦在此，豈皆為金革乎？ 皇太子今若抑哀，公除墨慘朝覲，歸至本院，依舊衰麻，酌於變通，庶可傳繼。」 宰臣然其議，遂命太常卿鄭叔則草奏，以冕議為是。 而穆質堅執前義，請依古禮，不妨太子墨衰於內也。 宰臣齊映、劉滋參酌群議，請依叔則之議，制從之。 及董晉為太常卿，德宗謂之曰：「皇太子所行周服，非朕本意，有諫官橫論之。 今熟計之，即禮官請依魏、晉故事，斯甚折衷。」 明年冬，上以太子久在喪，合至正月晦受吉服，欲以其年十一月釋衰麻，以及新正稱慶。 有司皆論不可，乃止。
The matter was referred to the Secretariat; the chief ministers summoned the ritual officials and asked, "The Analects says, 'When the Master ate beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill.' How can we now have the crown prince serve meals in sackcloth mourning until after the burial? According to statute, when officials wear unhemmed sackcloth, they are granted thirty days' leave and then publicly released from mourning. Measured against this regulation, reconsider the matter." Zhang Jian said, "I ask that we follow the Song and Qi precedent, when the empress mourned her parents with thirty days of public mourning followed by removal of dress, to set the crown prince's mourning periods." On the thirtieth day of public removal he would proceed to the inner court in dark mourning dress; on returning to his own residence he would wear sackcloth as before. Mu Zhi said, "Du Yuankai's argument for removing mourning dress after burial is not fit to serve as law. I believe that following the three-year system would be too heavy, while adopting the thirty-day variation would be too light; only by following the ancient way and fixing one year as the standard can it be settled." An edict ordered the chief ministers and ritual officials to determine what was acceptable. The chief ministers questioned the erudites on Mu Zhi's submission; Mian replied, "According to the Rites, three years of mourning make no distinction between noble and humble. How could mourning dress be graded according to whether one's parents were noble or humble? Moreover the Rites provide for removing unhemmed sackcloth at the public gate; the Kaiyuan Rites prescribe thirteen months of mourning when the empress mourns her parents, and following court instruction mourning is removed on the thirteenth day; the crown prince wears five months of mourning for maternal grandparents, and following court instruction it is removed on the fifth day. The reason is fear that serving in mourning dress would wound the supreme person's sensibilities. Therefore expedient regulations were adopted and clearly set forth in state statutes; removing sackcloth at the public gate has its meaning here too—surely it is not all because of military exigency? If the crown prince now suppresses grief, publicly removes mourning and attends court in dark dress, and on returning to his residence wears sackcloth as before, this balance of adaptation can be handed down." The chief ministers approved this opinion and ordered Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Zheng Shuzhe to draft the memorial, taking Mian's opinion as correct. But Mu Zhi firmly held to his earlier view and asked to follow the ancient rites, without preventing the crown prince from wearing dark mourning within. Chief ministers Qi Ying and Liu Zi weighed the various opinions and asked to follow Shuzhe's opinion; the regulation was adopted. When Dong Jin became Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Dezong told him, "The full-year mourning the crown prince is observing is not my original intent; remonstrance officials argued forcefully against it. On mature consideration, following the ritual officials' request to observe Wei and Jin precedent is a very balanced compromise." The next winter, because the crown prince had long been in mourning and should by the last day of the first month receive auspicious dress, the emperor wished to release sackcloth in the eleventh month so the new year could be celebrated. All the relevant offices argued it was impermissible, and the plan was abandoned.
84
六年十一月，上親行郊享。 上重慎祀典，每事依禮。 時冕為吏部郎中，攝太常博士，與司封郎中徐岱、倉部郎中陸質、工部郎中張薦，皆攝禮官，同修郊祀儀註，以備顧問。 初，詔以皇太子亞獻終獻，當受誓戒否，冕對曰：「準《開元禮》有之，然誓詞雲『不供其職，國有常刑』，今太子受誓，請改雲『各揚其職，肅奉常儀』。」 上又問升郊廟去劍履，及象劍尺寸之度，祝文輕重之宜，冕據禮經沿革聞奏，上甚嘉之。
In the eleventh month of the sixth year the emperor personally performed the suburban sacrifice. The emperor treated the sacrificial canon with great care and followed ritual in every detail. At that time Mian was Director in the Ministry of Appointments and acting Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices; together with Director in the Ministry of Seals Xu Dai, Director in the Ministry of Revenue Lu Zhi, and Director in the Ministry of Works Zhang Jian—all acting ritual officials—he jointly revised the suburban sacrifice protocol for consultation. Initially an edict asked whether the crown prince, as secondary and final offerer, should receive the oath of abstinence; Mian replied, "The Kaiyuan Rites provide for it, yet the oath text says, 'If one fails in his duty, the state has fixed punishments.' Since the crown prince receives the oath, I request changing it to read, 'Each shall perform his duty and reverently observe the regular rites.'" The emperor also asked about removing sword and shoes on ascending to the suburban altar and temple, the dimensions of ceremonial swords, and the proper weight of prayer texts; Mian reported according to the changes and continuities in the ritual classics, and the emperor greatly praised him.
85
冕言事頗切，執政不便之，出為婺州刺史。 十三年，兼御史中丞、福州刺史，充福建都團練觀察使。 冕在福州，奏置萬安監牧，於泉州界置群牧五，悉索部內馬五千七百匹、驢騾牛八百頭、羊三千口，以為監牧之資。 人情大擾，期年，無所滋息，詔罷之。 以政無狀，詔以閻濟美代歸而卒。 子璟，登進士第，亦以著述知名。
Mian's statements on affairs were quite pointed; the chief ministers found them inconvenient and sent him out as prefect of Wu. In the thirteenth year he was concurrently Vice Censor-in-Chief and prefect of Fuzhou, serving as defense commissioner and circuit supervisor of Fujian. While in Fuzhou, Mian memorialized to establish the Wan'an supervisory pasture; within Quanzhou he set up five group pastures, requisitioning throughout his jurisdiction five thousand seven hundred horses, eight hundred donkeys, mules, and cattle, and three thousand sheep as capital for the pasture. Popular sentiment was greatly disturbed; after a year there was no increase at all, and an edict abolished the project. Because his governance was without merit, an edict replaced him with Yan Jimei; he died on the return journey. His son Jing passed the jinshi examination and was also known for literary composition.
86
璟，寶歷初登進士第，三遷監察御史。 時郊廟告祭，差攝三公行事，多以雜品； 璟時監察，奏曰：「準開元二十三年敕，宗廟大祠，宜差左右丞相、嗣王、特進、少保、少傅、尚書、賓客、御史大夫。 又二十五年敕，太廟五享，差丞相、師傅、尚書、嗣、郡王通攝，餘司不在差限。 又元和四年敕，太廟告祭攝官，太尉以宰相充，其攝司空、司徒，以僕射、尚書、師傅充，餘司不在差限。 比來吏部因循，不守前後敕文，用人稍輕。 請自今年冬季，勒吏部準開元、元和敕例差官。」 從之。 再遷度支員外郎，轉吏部。 開成初，換庫部員外郎、知制誥，尋以本官充翰林學士。
Jing passed the jinshi examination at the opening of Baoli and was thrice promoted to Investigating Censor. At that time when suburban and temple sacrifices were announced, the acting officials assigned to perform the rites as the Three Dukes were mostly men of mixed rank; Jing, then an investigating censor, memorialized, "According to the edict of the twenty-third year of Kaiyuan, for great sacrifices at the ancestral temple the Left and Right Chancellors, heir apparent kings, specially advanced officials, Junior Guardian, Junior Mentor, ministers, guest of honor, and censor-in-chief should be assigned. Again, the edict of the twenty-fifth year: for the five offerings at the Imperial Ancestral Temple, the chancellor, mentor, minister, heir, and commandery kings should serve in general substitution; other offices are outside the limit of assignment. Again, the edict of the fourth year of Yuanhe: for announced sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple, the acting Grand Marshal is filled by the chancellor; acting Minister of Works and Minister of Education are filled by vice directors, ministers, and mentors; other offices are outside the limit of assignment. Recently the Ministry of Appointments has followed routine and not observed the earlier and later edicts; the men appointed have been somewhat unworthy. I request that from this winter onward the Ministry of Appointments be ordered to assign officials according to Kaiyuan and Yuanhe edict precedent." The request was adopted. He was promoted again to External Official in the Ministry of Revenue and transferred to the Ministry of Appointments. At the opening of Kaicheng he was transferred to External Official in the Ministry of Treasury and charged with drafting imperial documents; soon afterward he served in that office as Academician of the Hanlin Academy.
87
初，璟祖芳精於譜學，永泰中按宗正譜牒，自武德已來宗枝昭穆相承，撰皇室譜二十卷，號曰《永泰新譜》，自後無人修續。
Initially Jing's grandfather Fang was expert in genealogy; in the Yongtai era he examined the genealogical registers of the Court of the Imperial Clan, traced the imperial branches and generations from Wude onward, and compiled the Imperial Clan Genealogy in twenty scrolls, titled the New Yongtai Genealogy; afterward no one continued it.
88
璟因召對，言及圖譜事，文宗曰：「卿祖嘗為皇家圖譜，朕昨觀之，甚為詳悉。 卿檢永泰後試修續之。」 璟依芳舊式，續德宗後事，成十卷，以附前譜，仍詔戶部供紙筆廚料。 五年，拜中書舍人充職。 武宗朝，轉禮部侍郎，再司貢籍，時號得人。 子韜亦以進士擢第。
When Jing was summoned for audience and spoke of genealogical matters, Wenzong said, "Your grandfather once compiled the imperial genealogy; I read it yesterday and found it very detailed. Examine events after Yongtai and try to continue it." Jing followed Fang's old format, continued events after Dezong, and completed ten scrolls to append to the earlier genealogy; an edict also ordered the Ministry of Revenue to supply paper, brushes, and pantry provisions. In the fifth year he was appointed Secretariat Drafter and continued in that office. In the Wuzong reign he was transferred to Vice Minister of Rites and twice supervised the examination registry; at the time he was praised for selecting capable men. His son Tao also passed the jinshi examination.
89
沈傳師
Shen Chuanshi
90
沈傳師，字子言，吳人。 父既濟，博通群籍，史筆尤工，吏部侍郎楊炎見而稱之。 建中初，炎為宰相，薦既濟才堪史任，召拜左拾遺、史館修撰。 既濟以吳兢撰《國史》，以則天事立本紀，奏議非之曰：
Shen Chuanshi, styled Ziyan, was from Wu. His father Ji Ji was broadly versed in all books and especially skilled with the historiographer's brush; Vice Minister of Appointments Yang Yan saw him and praised him. At the opening of Jianzhong Yan became chancellor and recommended Ji Ji's talent for historiographical duty; he was summoned and appointed Left Remonstrance and Reviser and Compiler in the Historiography Institute. Because Wu Jing had compiled the National History and established a basic annal for Empress Wu Zetian's reign, Ji Ji submitted a memorial objecting:
91
史氏之作，本乎懲勸，以正君臣，以維家邦。 前端千古，後法萬代，使其生不敢差，死不妄懼。 緯人倫而經世道，為百王準的； 不止屬辭比事，以日系月而已。 故善惡之道，在乎勸誡； 勸誡之柄，存乎褒貶。 是以《春秋》之義，尊卑輕重升降，幾微仿佛，雖一字二字，必有微旨存焉。 況鴻名大統，其可以貸乎？
The historiographer's work is rooted in admonition and encouragement—to correct ruler and subject and to sustain family and state. It takes the front of a thousand ages and makes law for ten thousand generations, so that while living they dare not err and in death they dare not presume. It weaves human relations and threads the way of the world, serving as the standard for a hundred kings; it is not merely arranging words and comparing events, month following month. Thus the way of good and evil lies in admonition and warning; the handle of admonition and warning rests in praise and blame. Therefore the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals—in raising and lowering noble and humble, light and heavy, in the slightest shades—is that even in one or two characters a subtle intent must be preserved. How much more when it is a great name and supreme succession—can that be lent out?
92
伏以則天皇后，初以聰明睿哲，內輔時政，厥功茂矣。 及弘道之際，孝和以長君嗣位，而太后以專制臨朝； 俄又廢帝，或幽或徙。 既而握圖稱箓，移運革名，牝司燕啄之蹤，難乎備述。 其後五王建策，皇運復興，議名之際，得無降損。 必將義以親隱，禮從國諱，茍不及損，當如其常，安可橫絕彜典，超居帝籍？ 昔仲尼有言，必也正名，故夏、殷二代為帝者三十世矣，而周人通名之曰王； 吳、楚、越之君為王者百餘年，而《春秋》書之為子。 蓋高下自乎彼，而是非稽乎我。 過者抑之，不及者援之，不為弱減，不為僭奪。 握中持平，不振不傾，使其求不可得，而蓋不可掩，斯古君子所以慎其名也。
I respectfully observe that Empress Wu Zetian, by her intelligence and sagacity at first, assisted in governing from within, and her achievements were abundant. At the time of the Hongdao transition, Xiaozong as the elder sovereign succeeded to the throne, yet the empress dowager held sole rule over the court; soon she deposed the emperor, imprisoning or banishing him. Then she grasped the chart and claimed the succession, shifted the mandate and changed the dynastic name; the traces of a hen ruling and a swallow usurping are hard to recount in full. Afterward the Five Princes devised policy and the imperial fortune was revived; at the moment of deciding the name, could there be no lowering or reduction? If righteousness requires concealing kin and ritual follows state taboo, if it cannot reach the point of injury it should remain as usual—how can one recklessly sever the constant canon and leap above the register of emperors? Confucius once said, "One must rectify names"; thus though Xia and Shang had thirty generations of rulers called emperors, the Zhou uniformly named them kings; the rulers of Wu, Chu, and Yue were kings for more than a hundred years, yet the Spring and Autumn Annals records them as sons. High and low depend on them, but right and wrong are judged by us. Where there is excess, suppress it; where there is deficiency, support it—neither diminishing the weak nor seizing from the presumptuous. Holding the center level, neither stirring nor tilting, so that what is sought cannot be obtained yet what is covered cannot be hidden—this is how the ancient gentleman was careful with names.
93
夫則天體自坤順，位居乾極，以柔乘剛，天紀倒張，進以強有，退非德讓。 今史臣追書，當稱之太后，不宜曰「上」。 孝和雖迫母後之命，降居籓邸，而體元繼代，本吾君也，史臣追書，宜稱曰「皇帝」，不宜曰「廬陵王」。 睿宗在景龍已前，天命未集，徒稟後制，假臨大寶，於倫非次，於義無名，史臣書之，宜曰「相王」，未宜曰「帝」。 若以得失既往，遂而不舉，則是非褒貶，安所辨正，載筆執簡，謂之何哉？ 則天廢國家歷數，用周正朔，廢國家太廟，立周七廟。 鼎命革矣，徽號易矣，旂裳服色，既已殊矣！ 今安得以周氏年歷而列為《唐書》帝紀？ 征諸禮經，是謂亂名。 且孝和繼天踐祚，在太后之前，而敘年制紀，居太后之下； 方之躋僖。 是謂不智，詳今考古，並未為可。
Empress Wu by nature followed Kun's yielding yet occupied Qian's summit, using softness to overcome hardness; heaven's order was overturned, advancing by forcible possession and retreating without virtuous yielding. Now when historiographers write in retrospect they should call her Empress Dowager and should not say "Sovereign." Though Xiaozong was compelled by his mother's command and demoted to a princely residence, he embodied the origin and succeeded to the age—he is fundamentally our sovereign; historiographers writing in retrospect should call him "Emperor" and should not say "Prince of Luling." Before Jinglong Ruizong's mandate was not yet gathered; he merely received the empress dowager's command and temporarily held the great treasure—out of order in human relations and without name in righteousness; historiographers writing of him should say "Prince Regent" and should not yet say "Emperor." If because gain and loss are already past one lets it pass and does not raise it, then how are right and wrong, praise and blame, to be distinguished and corrected—what does it mean to hold the brush and keep the record? Empress Wu abolished the state's dynastic succession, adopted Zhou's calendar, abolished the state's Imperial Ancestral Temple, and established Zhou's seven temples. The mandate of the tripod was changed, imperial titles were altered, banners, robes, and colors of dress were already different! How can one now use Zhou's yearly chronology and list it as an imperial annal in the Book of Tang? Consulting the ritual classics, this is called disordering names. Moreover Xiaozong succeeded to heaven and took the throne before the empress dowager, yet in arranging years and fixing annals he is placed below the empress dowager; compared to elevating Duke Xi, this is called unwise. Examining the present against antiquity, none of it is acceptable.
94
或曰：班、馬良史也，編述漢事，立高後以續帝載，豈有非之者乎？ 答曰：昔高後稱制，因其曠嗣，獨有分王諸呂，負於漢約，無遷鼎革命之甚。 況其時孝惠已歿，孝文在下，宮中二子，非劉氏種，不紀呂後，將紀誰焉？ 雖雲其然，議者猶為不可，況遷鼎革命者乎？
Some say: Ban and Sima were fine historians; in compiling Han affairs they established Empress Gao to continue the imperial record—was there anyone who objected? The reply: In former times Empress Gao held sole rule because the heir's line was vacant; she alone enfeoffed the various Lüs, betraying Han's covenant—there was nothing so grave as shifting the tripod and transforming the mandate. Moreover at that time Emperor Xiaohui was already dead and Emperor Xiaowen was below; the two sons in the palace were not of the Liu clan—if Empress Lü were not recorded, whom would one record? Though one may say it was so, debaters still held it impermissible—how much more when the tripod is shifted and the mandate transformed?
95
或曰：若天後不紀，帝緒缺矣，則二十二年行事，何所系乎？ 曰：孝和以始年登大位，以季年復舊業，雖尊名中奪，而天命未改，足以首事，足以表年，何所拘閡，裂為二紀？ 昔魯昭之出也，《春秋》歲書其居，曰「公在乾侯」。 且君在，雖失位，不敢廢也。 今請並《天後紀》合《孝和紀》，每於歲首，必書孝和所在以統之，書曰某年春正月，皇帝在房陵，太后行某事，改某制云云。 則紀稱孝和，而事述太后，俾名不失正，而禮不違常； 名禮兩得，人無間矣！ 其姓氏名諱，入宮之由，歷位之資，才藝智略，年辰崩葬，別纂錄入《皇后傳》，列於廢後王庶人之下，題其篇曰「則天順聖武後」云。
Some say: If the empress dowager is not recorded, the imperial line is broken—then to what are twenty-two years of actions attached? The answer: Xiaozong at the first year ascended the great throne and at the last year restored the former enterprise; though his honored name was seized in the middle, the mandate of heaven was not changed—sufficient to head affairs and sufficient to mark the year; what constraint requires splitting it into two annals? In former times when Duke Zhao of Lu went into exile, the Spring and Autumn Annals each year recorded where he was, saying, "The Duke was at Ganhou." Moreover while the ruler lives, though he loses position, he is not abolished. I now request merging the Empress Dowager Annal with the Xiaozong Annal; at the head of each year one must record where Xiaozong was to unify it, writing: In such-and-such year, spring, first month, the emperor was at Fangling; the empress dowager performed such-and-such affair and changed such-and-such regulation, and so on. Then the annal would be titled Xiaozong while affairs would narrate the empress dowager, so that the name would not lose rectitude and ritual would not violate the constant; name and ritual both obtained, and no one would find fault! Her surname, personal name, taboo, the reason for entering the palace, qualifications for successive offices, talent, wisdom, and stratagem, year of birth, death, and burial should be separately compiled into the Biography of the Empress, placed below the deposed empress and commoner consorts, with the chapter title "Empress Zetian Shunsheng Wu."
96
事雖不行，而史氏稱之。
Though the proposal was not adopted, historians praised it.
97
德宗初即位，銳於求理。 建中二年夏，敕中書、門下兩省，分置待詔官三十員，以見官前任及同正試攝九品已上，擇文學理道、韜鈐法度之深者為之，各準品秩給俸錢，廩餼、幹力、什器、館宇之設，以公錢為之本，收息以贍用。 物論以為兩省皆名侍臣，足備顧問，無勞別置冗員。 既濟上疏論之曰：
When Dezong first ascended the throne he was keen to seek good governance. In summer of the second year of Jianzhong an edict ordered the Secretariat and Chancellery to each establish thirty awaiting-edict posts, drawn from former officials of rank nine and above in regular, probationary, and acting status who were skilled in letters, principles, military arts, and law—each receiving salary according to rank, with pantry provisions, laborers, utensils, and lodging established from public funds as capital, collecting interest to support expenses. Public opinion held that both bureaus already had attendant ministers sufficient for consultation and there was no need separately to establish superfluous posts. Ji Ji submitted a memorial arguing:
98
臣伏以陛下今日之理，患在官煩，不患員少； 患在不問，不患無人。 且中書、門下兩省常侍、諫議、補闕、拾遺，總四十員，及常參待制之官，日有兩人，皆備顧問，亦不少矣。 中有二十一員，尚闕人未充，他司缺職，累倍其數。 陛下若謂見官非才，不足與議，則當選求能者，以代其人。 若欲務廣聰明，畢收淹滯，則當擇其可者，先補缺員。 則朝無曠官，俸不徒費。 且夫置錢息利，是有司權宜，非陛下經理之法。 今官三十員，皆給俸錢，幹力及廚廩什器、建造廳宇，約計一月不減百萬，以他司息例準之，當以錢二千萬為之本，方獲百萬之利。 若均本配人，當復除二百戶，或許其入流。 反覆計之，所損滋甚。 當今關輔大病，皆為百司息錢，傷人破產，積於府縣。 實思改革，以正本源。 又臣嘗計天下財賦耗篸之大者，唯二事焉：最多者兵資，次多者官俸。 其餘雜費，十不當二事之一。 所以黎人重困，杼軸猶空。 方期緝熙，必藉裁減。 今四方形勢，兵罷未得，資費之廣，蓋非獲已。 陛下躬行儉約，節用愛人，豈俾閑官，復為冗食？ 籍舊而置，猶可省也，若之何加焉？ 陛下必以制出不可改，請重難慎擇，遷延寢罷。
Your subject respectfully observes that in Your Majesty's governance today the worry is that offices are too numerous, not that posts are too few; the worry is that inquiry is not made, not that there are no men. Moreover the Secretariat and Chancellery together have forty regular attendants, remonstrance and reviser, and remonstrance and reviser posts, and two officials on regular court attendance each day—all sufficient for consultation and not few. Among them twenty-one posts still lack men to fill them; other offices lack incumbents by many times that number. If Your Majesty thinks the current officials lack talent and are unfit for deliberation, then capable men should be sought to replace them. If Your Majesty wishes to extend intelligence widely and gather all the overlooked, then among those fit the vacancies should first be filled. Then the court would have no vacant offices and salaries would not be wasted. Moreover establishing capital to collect interest is an expedient of the relevant offices, not Your Majesty's method of governance. Now thirty posts all receive salaries, laborers, and pantry provisions, utensils, and construction of halls—estimated for one month not less than one million cash; measured against interest rates in other offices, capital of twenty million cash would be required to obtain one million in profit. If the capital were distributed per person, two hundred households would again have to be exempted, or they might be permitted entry into the official stream. Reckoned back and forth, the harm grows ever greater. Today the great illness of the capital region is that every office lends money at interest, injuring people and ruining households, accumulating in prefectures and counties. I truly wish for reform to rectify the root source. Moreover your subject once calculated the greatest drains on the empire's revenue and expenditure: of two matters, the most is military supplies, the next is official salaries. All other miscellaneous expenses do not equal one of these two. Therefore the common people are heavily afflicted and the loom is still empty. When one expects order and brilliance, one must rely on cutting and reducing. Now in the four directions the military situation has not yet ceased and expenses are broad—this is surely unavoidable. Your Majesty personally practices frugality, economizes expenditure, and cherishes the people—how can idle offices again become superfluous eaters? To establish them from the old registers could still be reduced—how then add more? If Your Majesty must hold that the regulation once issued cannot be changed, I request weighing the difficulty carefully, choosing with care, and deferring until it is abandoned.
99
其事竟不得行。 既而楊炎譴逐，既濟坐貶處州司戶。 後復入朝，位終禮部員外郎。
The matter in the end was not carried out. Soon afterward Yang Yan was punished and banished; Ji Ji was implicated and demoted to Registrar of Chuzhou. Later he reentered court and ended as External Official in the Ministry of Rites.
100
傳師擢進士，登制科乙第，授太子校書郎、鄠縣尉，直史館，轉左拾遺、左補闕，並兼史職。 遷司門員外郎、知制誥，召充翰林學士。 歷司勛、兵部郎中，遷中書舍人。 性恬退無競，時翰林未有承旨，次當傳師為之，固稱疾，宣召不起，乞以本官兼史職。 俄兼御史中丞，出為潭州刺史、湖南觀察使。 入為尚書右丞。 出為洪州刺史、江南西道觀察使，轉宣州刺史、宣歙池觀察使。 入為吏部侍郎。 太和元年卒，年五十九，贈吏部尚書。
Chuanshi passed the jinshi examination and ranked in the second class of the decree examination; he was appointed Proofreader of the Crown Prince and aide of E County, direct appointment to the Historiography Institute, transferred to Left Remonstrance and Reviser and Left Reviser—all concurrently historiographical posts. He was promoted to External Official in the Ministry of Justice and charged with drafting imperial documents, and was summoned to serve as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. He served successively as Director in the Ministries of Merit and War and was promoted to Secretariat Drafter. By nature retiring and without contention, at that time the Hanlin Academy had no chief drafter and Chuanshi was next in line; he firmly pleaded illness, would not rise when summoned by imperial order, and begged to hold his current office concurrently with historiographical duty. Soon he was concurrently Vice Censor-in-Chief and sent out as prefect of Tan and circuit supervisor of Hunan. He returned to court as Right Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue. He was sent out as prefect of Hong and circuit supervisor of Jiangxi, transferred to prefect of Xuan and circuit supervisor of Xuan, She, and Chi. He returned to court as Vice Minister of Appointments. In the first year of Taihe he died, aged fifty-nine; posthumously honored as Minister of Appointments.
101
初，傳師父既濟撰《建中實錄》十卷，為時所稱。 傳師在史館，預修《憲宗實錄》未成，廉察湖南，特詔賫一分史稿，成於理所。
Initially Chuanshi's father Ji Ji compiled the Jianzhong Veritable Record in ten scrolls, praised at the time. While Chuanshi was in the Historiography Institute he participated in compiling the Xianzong Veritable Record, which was unfinished; when he was made supervisory commissioner of Hunan, a special edict sent him one portion of the historiographical draft, and he completed it in his prefecture.
102
有子樞、詢，皆登進士第。
He had sons Shu and Xun; both passed the jinshi examination.
103
詢歷清顯，中書舍人、翰林學士、禮部侍郎。 咸通中，檢校戶部尚書、潞州長史、昭義節度使。 為政簡易，性本恬和。 奴歸秦者，通詢侍者，詢將戮之未果； 奴結牙將為亂，夜攻府第，詢舉家遇害。
Xun held clear and eminent posts: Secretariat Drafter, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, and Vice Minister of Rites. In the Xiantong era he served as acting Minister of Revenue, Chief Administrator of Lu Prefecture, and military commissioner of Zhaoyi. His governance was simple and easy; by nature he was fundamentally mild and harmonious. A slave named Gui Qin had relations with Xun's attendants; Xun intended to execute him but did not succeed; the slave joined with the garrison officers to raise disorder, attacked the prefectural residence by night, and Xun's entire household was killed.
104
史臣曰
The historiographer comments
105
史臣曰：前代以史為學者，率不偶於時，多罹放逐，其故何哉？ 誠以褒貶是非在於手，賢愚輕重系乎言，君子道微，俗多忌諱，一言切己，嫉之如仇。 所以峘、薦坎壈於仕塗，沈、柳不登於顯貫，後之載筆執簡者，可以為之痛心！ 道在必伸，物不終否，子孫藉其餘祐，多至公卿者，蓋有天道存焉！
The historiographer comments: Scholars who took history as their study in former ages mostly did not meet with fortune in their times and often suffered banishment—why is this? Truly because praise and blame, right and wrong, rest in the hand, and the weight of worthy and unworthy hangs on words—when the gentleman's way is slight and the vulgar are full of taboo, one word that cuts to the self is hated like an enemy. Therefore Han and Zhang suffered hardship on the official road, and Shen and Liu did not reach eminent rank—later men who hold the brush and keep the record may grieve for them! The Way must extend; things do not end in denial—their descendants relied on their remaining blessing and many reached the rank of chief minister; surely the Way of Heaven is preserved therein!
106
贊曰：褒貶以言，孔道是模。 誅亂以筆，亦有董狐。 邦家大典，班、馬何辜？ 懲惡勸善，史不可無。
In praise it is said: Praise and blame lie in words; the way of Confucius is the model. To punish disorder with the brush—there is also a Dong Hu. The great canon of state and family—what wrong did Ban and Sima commit? To punish evil and encourage good—history cannot be absent.
